shared_materials.text:
When a coastal town replaced its ageing public clocks, officials expected the new synchronised displays to end complaints about late buses. The clocks became accurate, but the complaints continued. A subsequent survey showed that passengers cared less about the exact minute than about whether a promised service arrived at all. The transport office had been measuring departures from the depot, while residents were describing arrivals at stops. Neither account was fabricated; the two groups were answering different questions.

Instead of buying another display system, the town published a simple stop-by-stop service log. Drivers could annotate delays, and passengers could report missing journeys. The first month produced more complaints, which opponents called evidence of failure. Yet many of these complaints concerned disruptions that had previously gone unrecorded. Over the following months, the shared record helped staff identify a recurring scheduling conflict. The lesson was not that technology was useless. It was that a precise measurement could still miss the experience it was meant to represent, and that making a problem visible might temporarily make the statistics look worse.

An archive is useful not merely because it preserves documents, but because it makes their origins (1) ___. A note without a date may still be valuable, (2) ___ its claims must be read cautiously. Archivists therefore record the context in which an item was produced, rather than treating every surviving sheet as (3) ___ reliable. Such work does not eliminate uncertainty; it gives readers the means to (4) ___ it. The aim is not to replace judgement (5) ___ a catalogue, but to make judgement better informed.
